claims.feature: other: competing versions of one story
claims.claim: Kay says the vast gulf between how the Uskoks were seen by Venice and Dubrovnik and how they understood themselves is very fertile ground for a novelist.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Chris Urie, Clarkesworld issue 117
claims.quote: That kind of gap is very fertile ground for a novelist

claims.feature: other: under-explored corners of the record
claims.claim: Kay says he likes finding corners of history that have been under-explored.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Chris Urie, Clarkesworld issue 117
claims.quote: I like finding corners of history that have been under-explored

claims.feature: other: not talking down to the reader
claims.claim: Kay says he is drawn to intelligent characters and gets irritated if he feels too much smarter than the characters, unless that is done with purpose.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Patrick St-Denis (fantasyhotlist)
claims.quote: I get irritated if I feel too much smarter than the characters

claims.claim: McBean writes that in Kay's dialogue emotion is often conveyed by what is not said.
claims.source: Chris McBean, The Rowanwood Chronicles blog, 24 December 2025
claims.quote: Emotion is often conveyed by what is not said.

claims.feature: other: worldview rendered as the inhabitants hold it
claims.claim: Kay says the fantastic lets him make the world be as his characters believe it to be.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, Los Angeles Review of Books, 14 August 2016
claims.quote: make the world be as my characters believe it to be
claims.page: answer to 'How else does the fantastic serve your purposes?'

claims.feature: other: worldview rendered as the inhabitants hold it
claims.claim: Kay says a modern reader tends to a smug, patronising attitude toward the past, and that presenting the world as the characters believe it removes that smugness.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, Los Angeles Review of Books, 14 August 2016
claims.quote: it removes that smugness from the reader
claims.page: answer to 'How else does the fantastic serve your purposes?'

claims.claim: Kay says he has used two moons in several books as a signal to the reader that the setting is not our world.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, Los Angeles Review of Books, 14 August 2016
claims.quote: The two moons say, We’re not here
claims.page: answer about setting the rules of engagement

claims.claim: Kay says that if a reader can pick out what is made up and what is real, the storytelling has been botched.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, Los Angeles Review of Books, 14 August 2016
claims.quote: if a reader can pick out what’s made up and what’s real
claims.page: answer about the Hilary Mantel review

claims.claim: Kay says the past is, for him, staggeringly alien, and that writers about the past should acknowledge and work with that.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, Los Angeles Review of Books, 14 August 2016
claims.quote: it’s also, for me, staggeringly alien

claims.claim: The interviewer Christine Fischer Guy writes that a reverence for language runs through everything Kay writes.
claims.source: Christine Fischer Guy (interviewer's framing), Los Angeles Review of Books, 14 August 2016
claims.quote: A reverence for language runs through everything he writes.

claims.feature: other: minor lives as world texture

claims.feature: other: magic quantity across the oeuvre
claims.claim: Walton describes a trajectory away from magic across Kay's books, with Fionavar full of magic, Tigana less, Arbonne less again, and The Lions of Al-Rassan containing nothing but an accurate prophecy.
Nepveu identifies a throw-away line in the prologue of Sailing to Sarantium, a sandalmaker's having seen a ghost, as the first signal that the book is not a straight historical.
claims.quote: a throw-away line in the prologue is the first signal

claims.claim: The Speculiction reviewer identifies as a habit of Kay's middle period numerous throwaway lines that flash forward to a later consequence.

claims.quote: there are numerous throwaway lines to the effect
